claims.claim: An editor's first-50 review credits titled POV chapters with removing head-hopping confusion and praises exposition delivered in scene.
claims.quote: giving each character a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably

claims.claim: Description flows without Tolkien-style descriptive excess and each character keeps a distinct voice.
claims.quote: fluid lyricism, without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium

claims.claim: Sanderson's lecture uses 'Bran Stark' in chapter one as a tone promise of bleakness.
Ser, southron, and craven date to 1451, 1488, and 1400; turncloak is an archaic-sounding remake of turncoat; 'butt' and 'ass' jar.
Different cultures are marked by colloquial phrases and aphorisms such as 'words are wind'.
Martin uses accurate late-Middle-English words sparingly, avoids thou/thee, and keeps modern syntax.
claims.quote: sweet spot between Modern and Middle English

claims.feature: lexical cohesion and register by class
claims.claim: Repeated insult words bind paragraphs, 'without' means outside, and m'Lord versus my Lord marks class; lexical density about 4–4.5 and a sixth-grade readability index.
Text-mining across four series finds Martin uses -ly adverbs least and reads at about age ten by readability index.
claims.source: Winter Is Coming (Dan Selcke) on Dimitris Spathis, 2015-09-24

claims.claim: AGOT scores Flesch Reading Ease 87, has 851 sentences over 30 words, 3.39% slow-paced paragraphs, and near-equal standard versus alternative dialogue tags with adverbs in tags flagged.
claims.source: AutoCrit, 'What's the Score? A Game of Thrones'

claims.claim: 'Mummer's farce' recurs constantly and 'jape' reads as a pretentious substitute for joke; prose 'borders on serviceable'.
claims.quote: at least ten times in every book

claims.claim: Hodor's and Reek's repeated lines become formula rather than characterisation.
Sex scenes fixate on nipple size and colour and crude similes, unlike his assured violence and heraldry.
claims.quote: not good at writing about sex

claims.claim: Feasts are rendered as course-by-course lists with taste and smell, and appetite indexes a character's mental state.
Meal descriptions mark inclusion, class, and culture, with sensory verbs carrying the emotion.
Martin describes loving a Tyrion chapter, then rereading it and deciding it failed.
claims.quote: I wrote a Tyrion chapter I just loved

verdicts.trueWording: While shifting POV can occasionally lead to confusion, giving each character a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Exposition-in-scene praise also present: 'By giving us needed information in the form of dialogue and scenes, Martin holds our attention.' Byline Shannon Roberts confirmed; piece marks AGOT's 20th anniversary (=2016), though the page footer stamp reads 2024-01-07.

verdicts.trueWording: accounts of the mythic world unfold with fluid lyricism, without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Distinct-voice half confirmed in the same paragraph: Martin gives 'each character their own unique voice'. Date 2012-06-07 matches the URL path.

verdicts.trueWording: naming his viewpoint character Bran Stark in the first chapter of A Game of Thrones is a tone promise. The name Stark implies a bleak and grim mood
verdicts.note: Quote exact and the bleakness gloss is explicit. Byline Heba Hallak, Apr 15 2026, confirmed on the page; it reports Sanderson's BYU lecture.

verdicts.trueWording: which is Martin's archaic-sounding amendment of turncoat
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Every other element confirmed on the page: 'Ser for Sir, Southron for Southern, and craven meaning cowardly all date from 1451, 1488, and 1400 respectively, according to the Oxford English Dictionary', and 'modern-sounding terms such as butt and ass jarring'.

verdicts.trueWording: portrayed through a number of colloquial phrases
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied, so substance only. Page: the flavour of the different languages of the seven kingdoms is 'portrayed through a number of colloquial phrases', and '"Words are wind" is another aphorism used by the characters'. Page says languages/kingdoms where the claim says cultures.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin hits a sweet spot between Modern and Middle English
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Rest confirmed verbatim: 'While choosing not to use Middle English pronouns and using mostly modern syntax, Martin gives A Game of Thrones a historical feel by using accurate 1400s archaic diction'; 'Martin uses these words sparingly'. Author Delane Just, Jan 22 2018.

verdicts.trueWording: For instance, terms like "elsewise" (A Feast For Crows, p. 2742) could hardly be found in any story set in modern times
verdicts.note: Words match exactly; only the capital T and the single-quote style differ from the page's mid-sentence 'terms like "elsewise"'. All four sub-claims confirmed: lexical cohesion via the repeated insult ('repeated five times', 'ties parts of a text'); 'without' in 'the old English meaning "outside [the wall]"'; m'Lord vs my Lord by birth; density 'between 4 and 4.5'; 'The ARI score for A Game of Thrones is sixth-grade, or 11-12 years old'.

verdicts.trueWording: What does this chart tell us? That George R.R. Martin hates adverbs.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Four series confirmed (LOTR, Harry Potter, Hunger Games, ASOIAF) and 'you only need to be 10 years old to understand A Song of Ice and Fire'. Caveat: the page never says '-ly' adverbs nor the word 'least' - it credits an adverb chart hosted on Spathis' own Medium post.

verdicts.trueWording: a Game of Thrones comes in with a Flesch Reading Ease score of 87
verdicts.note: Quote exact and all three further figures confirmed: 'a comparatively small 851 sentences containing more than 30 words'; 'A tiny 3.39% of A Game of Thrones is detected as slower in pace'; 'having almost the same number of alternative dialogue tags as we do the standard two is a little alarming'; and a section flagging 'Martin's use of adverbs in dialogue tags'.

verdicts.trueWording: seriously, the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book
verdicts.note: Quote exact, about 'mummer's farce'. 'Jape' confirmed: 'Jape, aside from its pretentiousness, is a singularly displeasing word.' The prose verdict is on the page but differently worded and misspelled there: 'Most of the time his prose borders on the servicable' - the claim's 'borders on serviceable' is a paraphrase, not a quotation.

verdicts.trueWording: Annoying speech mannerisms... sometimes his choices are inexplicable
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied. Page devotes a section to Hodor's one-word dialogue (a mock exchange ending 'HOOOOOOODOOOOOOOOR') and to Reek's rhyme, 'Reek, my name is Reek, it rhymes with [random word]', framing both as mechanical repetition rather than characterisation.

verdicts.trueWording: George R.R. Martin is good at writing about violence and heraldry. He is not good at writing about sex.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Nipples confirmed: 'Nipples of massive girth, darkness, and circumference: Martin is obsessed with them', with 'big dark', 'huge dark', 'fat'/'brown', 'wide pink circles'. Crude similes confirmed: 'Myrish swamp', 'fat pink mast'. Byline Joe Streckert, April 2 2014; note the live URL now redirects to portlandmercury.com/general/the-erotica-of-westeros-12111961/.

verdicts.trueWording: tonight all the food was flavored with fear
verdicts.note: Quote exact (Martin's line as quoted in the piece). Course-by-course cataloguing confirmed ('All the while the courses came and went... Then came trout fresh from the river'), and the appetite claim is explicit: 'Martin uses people's reaction to food a lot to show state of mind.'

verdicts.trueWording: uses food to establish the emotional states of his characters
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied. Belonging/class confirmed ('a sign of brotherhood, of the sense of fraternity'; Jon as bastard 'not fit to sit in the main hall'), culture confirmed ('Dothraki food, drink, and the way they celebrate tell us quite a bit about them as a group'). 'Sensory verbs' is the analyst's gloss, not the page's wording. Byline note: page credits 'By Andrea Guzman' in the body under poster Isabel Carrasco, translated by Oliver G. Alvar; date April 9 2019 matches.

verdicts.trueWording: I wrote a Tyrion chapter I just loved... Then I looked at it and said: 'I can't do this, it will change the whole book.'
verdicts.note: Quote exact. The 'reread and decided it failed' half is the page's next clause. Author 'Matt', Jan 30 2026, confirmed on the page; it quotes Martin on The Winds of Winter.
